content: The prevalence of oral candidiasis in HIV-infected children can reach as high as 81%, as noted in personal communication by Christine Henneberg in 2010. If left untreated, these lesions significantly contribute to the morbidity associated with HIV infection, as highlighted by Oude Lashof in 2004. Preventing and treating HIV-associated oral candidiasis is essential for maintaining the quality of life in affected individuals. The clinical manifestations of oral candidiasis include a soft white coating or pseudomembrane on the mucosal surfaces of the mouth, which reveals a red, raw surface when wiped off. Other presentations include depapillation or a red/raw surface on the tongue, or thick white plaques that cannot be rubbed off, which are diagnostically challenging. While Candida albicans is the most commonly implicated organism, other species have also been identified. In patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) may suggest Candida esophagitis, which requires endoscopy for definitive diagnosis. Most patients with esophageal candidiasis respond to antifungal therapy within three to seven days, as noted by Rabeneck and Laine in 1994. If there is no improvement with systemic antifungal therapy, endoscopy is indicated to rule out other causes of esophagitis, such as herpes simplex virus or cytomegalovirus, which are common in immunocompromised populations. For adults, oral fluconazole at a dose of 100–150 mg for 7–14 days is the preferred treatment. If fluconazole is unavailable or contraindicated, alternatives include topical therapy with nystatin suspension or pastilles, or clotrimazole troches. In children, oral fluconazole at 3 mg/kg for 7–14 days is recommended. For mild oropharyngeal candidiasis in children, topical therapy with nystatin suspension or pastilles (or clotrimazole troches) is advised. These recommendations are supported by strong evidence, though the quality of evidence varies. Prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all HIV-infected individuals with oropharyngeal candidiasis, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, and children. If there is no response to fluconazole after 14 days, a higher dose should be considered, and resistance to fluconazole should be evaluated. Itraconazole may be an alternative, but drug interactions must be carefully managed. In cases of esophageal candidiasis, treatment duration may need to be extended to 14–30 days. Maintenance therapy is not recommended. Gentian violet is no longer recommended due to lack of efficacy based on clinical experience. In HIV-infected patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis, a history of dysphagia should always be assessed to rule out esophageal candidiasis, which requires systemic antifungal treatment. Adequate hydration and nutrition should be ensured alongside drug therapy. These recommendations also apply to HIV-negative children and adults. A systematic review of antifungal treatments for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV-infected individuals found that fluconazole is highly effective, with efficacy rates ranging from 87% to 100%. It is more effective than ketoconazole and itraconazole due to better absorption and fewer drug interactions. However, the potential for resistance and the cost of prophylaxis limit the feasibility of widespread implementation. Antifungal prophylaxis is not recommended for oropharyngeal candidiasis. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are rare but life-threatening cutaneous disorders characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis. Mortality rates for SJS range from 1% to 5%, while TEN has a mortality rate of 25% to 30%. In HIV-infected patients, these conditions can occur both on and off ART. Common drugs causing adverse cutaneous reactions in HIV-infected patients include sulfonamides, antituberculosis drugs (especially thiacetazone), amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, clindamycin, and thalidomide. SJS is defined as detachment of less than 10% of body surface area (BSA) with widespread erythematous or purpuric macules or atypical target lesions. TEN involves detachment of more than 30% BSA, with or without spots. The overlap between SJS and TEN is defined as detachment of 10–30% BSA with widespread erythematous, purpuric, or atypical target-like lesions. Management of SJS and TEN involves discontinuation of the inciting medication and supportive care. The effectiveness of specific interventions, such as corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), remains controversial. Supportive care includes intravenous fluids, sepsis monitoring, wound care, dietary support, and management of complications such as eye and vaginal involvement. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended. ART initiation should be approached cautiously in patients not already on therapy. There is no reliable laboratory test to identify the offending drug; diagnosis is based on patient history and the temporal relationship of suspected drugs. The evidence for treatment of SJS and TEN in HIV-infected individuals is limited to case-control and cohort studies, with no randomized controlled trials available. Observational studies likely overestimate the true effect of treatment approaches, and all evidence is considered of very low quality. Further research is needed to evaluate treatment and prevention strategies for oropharyngeal candidiasis and SJS/TEN in HIV-infected populations, particularly in children and adolescents.
